title: GED RLA Introduction & Diagnostic
intro: You learn how the RLA test works: its parts, its time, its question types and its passing score. You learn a four-step method for every reading question. Then the workbook shows your strong skills and the skills to practise.

blocks.p: RLA means **Reasoning Through Language Arts**. It is one of the four GED® subjects. It tests three things: how well you read, how well you judge an argument, and how well you use written English.

head: Fact
What it means for you
rows: 150 minutes
This is the full test time. It includes a short time for instructions and a final review.
3 sections
You finish one section before you start the next one.
One 10-minute break
The break comes between two sections. Stand up, drink water, rest your eyes.
1 extended response
This is a written essay. You have 45 minutes for it.
Passing score: 145
You need 145 or higher. You need 145 on each of the four GED subjects.

blocks.p: The test has three topic areas: **reading for meaning**, **identifying and creating arguments**, and **grammar and language**.

blocks.remember: 150 minutes. 3 sections. One 10-minute break. One essay of 45 minutes. Pass at 145.

blocks.tip: A score of 165 to 174 shows you are ready for college-level courses. A score of 175 to 200 may earn college credit. First, aim for 145.

blocks.p: The test is on a computer. You do not only choose A, B, C or D. You also move, tap and choose from a list. You practise every type on this site.

head: Type
What you do
rows: Multiple choice
Read four answers. Choose the best one.
Drag and drop
Move items into the correct box or the correct order.
Drop-down
Open a small list inside a sentence. Choose the correct words.
Select an area (hot spot)
Tap the correct part of a text or picture.
Extended response
Read two passages. Write an essay.

blocks.p: On this site, you also practise **fill in the blank**, where you type a word or number. Other GED subjects use this type, so it is good practice.

blocks.mistake: Leaving a question with no answer. A blank answer is always wrong. If you are not sure, remove the answers that cannot be right, choose the best one, and go on.

blocks.p: You read two kinds of text.

list: **Informational texts** give facts or opinions about real life. Examples: an article, a letter, a workplace notice, a speech.
**Literary texts** tell a story. You read about characters, their feelings and their choices.

blocks.p: The passages start short and become longer. The questions do not test your memory. Every answer comes from the passage in front of you.

blocks.remember: You do not need to know the topic before the test. You need to read carefully and find proof in the passage.

blocks.p: The extended response is one essay. You have 45 minutes.

steps: You read two passages. They give two different arguments about one topic.
You decide which argument has more convincing evidence.
You write an essay that explains why. You use evidence from both passages.

blocks.passage: Passage 1 says the city should build more bicycle lanes. Passage 2 says the city should not.
blocks.title: Example task

blocks.weak: I think bicycle lanes are a good idea because I like cycling and it is healthy.
blocks.label: response
blocks.note: This gives the writer's own opinion. It does not look at the two passages.

blocks.strong: Passage 1 gives the stronger argument. It uses accident numbers from three cities, but Passage 2 gives only one person's story.
blocks.label: response
blocks.note: This judges the two arguments. It points to the evidence in each passage.

blocks.mistake: Writing your own opinion about the topic. The task asks which argument is **better supported**. It does not ask which side you like.

blocks.p: You learn the essay step by step in Sessions 7 to 10.
Use these four steps for every reading question.

steps: **Read the question first.** Now you know what to look for.
**Read the passage.** Read all of it. Do not skip the last lines.
**Find the evidence.** Find the words in the passage that prove the answer.
**Answer.** Choose the answer that matches the evidence.

blocks.passage: The town library used to close at 5 p.m. Most workers could not visit it. Last year, the library began to stay open until 9 p.m. on weekdays. Visits rose by forty percent.
blocks.title: Passage

blocks.question: Why did visits to the library rise?

blocks.note: The passage does not say this. It is a guess from real life.

blocks.strong: Because the library now stays open later, so workers can visit.
blocks.note: This uses two facts from the passage: workers could not visit before 5 p.m., and the library now closes at 9 p.m.

blocks.remember: The answer is in the passage. Point to the line that proves it.

blocks.mistake: Choosing an answer because it is true in real life. It must be true **in the passage**.

blocks.p: Many students know the answers but do not finish. A plan for your time protects your score.

blocks.weak: I will answer every question perfectly. I will stay on a hard question until I get it.
blocks.label: plan
blocks.note: One hard question can take the time of five easy ones.

blocks.strong: I answer the questions I know first. If a question takes too long, I choose my best answer, mark it, and come back if I have time.
blocks.label: plan
blocks.note: Every question gets an answer, and easy points are not lost.

list: Look at the clock after each passage, not after each question.
Do not spend a long time on one question. Choose, mark it, move on.
In the essay, keep a few minutes at the end to check your writing.
Use the 10-minute break. A rested mind reads faster.

blocks.tip: These pacing ideas are advice from your teacher. They are not official GED rules.

blocks.p: A diagnostic shows where you are now. It is not a pass or fail test. The workbook in this session is your diagnostic.
It checks these skills: test format, main idea, details, inference, vocabulary in context, author's purpose, argument and evidence, and grammar.

steps: Do the workbook alone. Do not use a dictionary or a translator.
Submit it. Read the **why** for every question, also the ones you got right.
Look at the two lists: your strong skills and your skills to practise.
Write the skills to practise in your notebook. You will watch them improve.

blocks.remember: A low diagnostic score is useful. It tells you and Ms. Maria what to work on first.

glossary: a short text that you read in the test
the essay in the RLA test
an opinion with reasons and evidence to support it
facts or words from the text that prove an idea
the most important point of a text
a small fact that supports the main idea
an idea that the text does not say directly, but that the evidence shows
the reason the author wrote the text: to inform, to persuade, to entertain or to explain
finding the meaning of a word from the words around it
a text about real life, such as an article, a letter or a notice
a first check that shows your strong and weak skills
using your time well, so that you finish the test

workbook.q: How long is the GED RLA test?
workbook.why: The RLA test is 150 minutes. The other times belong to Social Studies (70), Science (90) and Math (115).

workbook.q: Choose the correct numbers.
workbook.text: The RLA test has {0} sections. You get one {1}-minute break. You have {2} minutes to write the essay.
workbook.why: RLA has 3 sections, one 10-minute break and 45 minutes for the extended response.

workbook.q: Type the number.
workbook.text: To pass the RLA test, you need a score of {0} or higher.
workbook.why: The passing score is 145 on each GED subject.

workbook.q: Which of these are part of the RLA test? Put each item in the correct box.
targets: Not part of the RLA test
workbook.why: The RLA test has reading questions, language questions and one essay. It has no speaking and no listening part.

workbook.passage: Hana works in a shop from Sunday to Thursday. She has no time to study after work, because she cooks for her family. So she studies on the bus. The ride takes forty minutes each way. She reads one page of her workbook on every ride.
workbook.q: When does Hana study?
workbook.why: The passage says, "So she studies on the bus." She has no time after work, and the passage does not talk about Friday.

workbook.passage: Many adults return to study after years of work. They bring useful habits with them. They arrive on time, they ask questions, and they finish what they start.
workbook.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Adult students bring helpful habits to their studies.
workbook.why: Sentence 2 gives the main idea: adults bring useful habits. Sentence 3 only lists examples. "Arrive on time" is one detail, not the whole idea.

workbook.q: Tap the sentence that explains WHY the neighbours started the garden.
sentences: The empty land behind Block 12 was full of rubbish for years.
The neighbours wanted a clean, safe place for their children to play.
In March, they cleared the land and planted vegetables.
Now forty families share the garden.
workbook.why: Only sentence 2 gives the reason: they wanted a clean, safe place for their children. Sentence 1 describes the problem. Sentences 3 and 4 tell what happened later.

workbook.passage: The manager gave a brief talk before the shift. It lasted only two minutes, and then everyone went back to work.
workbook.q: What does the word "brief" mean in the passage?
workbook.why: The next sentence is the clue: the talk "lasted only two minutes". So "brief" means short.

workbook.q: Choose the correct verb for each sentence.
workbook.text: Every student in the class {0} a workbook. The students {1} the answers after they submit.
workbook.why: "Every student" is singular, so the verb is "has". "The students" is plural, so the verb is "see". The subject and the verb must agree.

workbook.passage: Omar looked out of the window and frowned. He took his long coat from the cupboard and put an umbrella in his bag. Then he left for work ten minutes early.
workbook.q: What can you infer from the passage?
workbook.why: The passage never says "rain". But Omar looks outside, frowns, and takes a coat and an umbrella. These clues show that he expects rain. He leaves early, so he is not late.

workbook.passage: The water in Building C will be turned off on Tuesday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Workers will repair a pipe on the second floor. Please fill containers with water before 9 a.m. We are sorry for the trouble. For questions, call the building office.
workbook.q: Why did the author write this notice?
options: To persuade residents to use less water
To inform residents about a planned water shut-off
To entertain residents with a story about a pipe
workbook.why: The notice gives facts: the day, the time, the reason and what to do. Its purpose is to inform. It does not try to change anyone's opinion.

workbook.q: Is each sentence a fact or an opinion? Put each one in the correct box.
items: The bus fare rose from 2 riyals to 3 riyals in January.
Buses are the best way to travel in a city.
The new timetable has twelve buses each hour.
workbook.why: You can check a fact: a price, a date, a number. "Best" and "ugly" are judgments. Different people can disagree about them, so they are opinions.

workbook.passage: Leila read the letter twice. Then she folded it carefully and put it in the drawer under her old photographs. At dinner, her brother asked about her day. "Nothing special," she said, and passed him the bread. She did not look up from her plate.
workbook.q: What does the passage suggest about Leila?
options: She is bored by the letter.
She wants to keep the letter private.
She is angry with her brother.
workbook.why: Leila hides the letter under photographs, says "Nothing special" and does not look up. These actions show that she does not want to talk about it. Nothing in the passage shows anger or boredom.

workbook.passage: All kitchen staff must attend the food safety training on Monday. The training is mandatory. Staff who do not attend cannot work in the kitchen until they complete it.
workbook.q: Find the word.
workbook.text: The word in the memo that means "required" is {0}.
workbook.why: The memo says staff "must attend" and cannot work without it. These clues show that "mandatory" means required.

workbook.q: Choose the correct words to complete the notice.
workbook.text: The clinic opens at 8 a.m.{0} it closes at 6 p.m. The doctors say {1} going to add evening hours next month.
workbook.why: Two complete sentences are joined with a comma and "and". A comma alone is an error. "They're" means "they are", which fits "they are going to add".

workbook.passage:
Our city council plans to end night bus service after 10 p.m. in order to save money. This decision would be a serious mistake. According to the transport office's own report, about 6,000 people ride the night buses each week, and more than half of them are travelling to or from work. Hospital cleaners, restaurant staff and security guards do not finish at five o'clock. If the buses stop, many of these workers will have to pay for taxis that cost ten times the bus fare, or give up their jobs.

Supporters of the plan say the night buses are often half empty. That is true, but it misses the point. A half-empty bus at midnight still carries twenty people who have no other way home. The council should look for savings that do not strain the workers who keep this city running at night.
workbook.q: What is the author's main claim?
options: Night buses are often half empty.
The city council should not end night bus service.
Taxis are too expensive for most people.
The transport office wrote a report about buses.
workbook.why: The claim is the opinion the author wants you to accept: ending night buses "would be a serious mistake". The other answers are details that the author uses, not the main claim.

workbook.q: Tap the sentence that gives the strongest evidence for the author's claim.
sentences: This decision would be a serious mistake.
According to the transport office's own report, about 6,000 people ride the night buses each week, and more than half of them are travelling to or from work.
Hospital cleaners, restaurant staff and security guards do not finish at five o'clock.
The council should look for savings that do not strain the workers who keep this city running at night.
workbook.why: Strong evidence can be checked. Sentence 2 gives numbers from an official report. Sentence 1 and sentence 4 are opinions. Sentence 3 is an example, but it has no numbers and no source.

workbook.q: The author writes, "That is true, but it misses the point." What can you infer about the author?
options: The author thinks the supporters are lying about empty buses.
The author accepts the supporters' fact but thinks it does not prove their argument.
The author agrees that the night buses should stop.
The author has never used a night bus.
workbook.why: "That is true" shows the author accepts the fact. "But it misses the point" shows the author thinks the fact does not support ending the service. Good writers often answer the other side in this way.

workbook.q: In the last sentence of the letter, what does "strain" mean?
options: To put pressure or difficulty on
workbook.why: "Strain" has several meanings. Here it is about workers who would pay more or lose their jobs. So it means to put pressure or difficulty on them. Always test the meaning in the sentence.

workbook.q: Why does the author name hospital cleaners, restaurant staff and security guards?
options: To show that the plan would hurt real workers with necessary jobs
To prove that these workers earn very little money
To explain how the transport office counts riders
To suggest that these workers should change their hours
workbook.why: Naming real jobs helps the reader picture who rides at night. It supports the claim that the plan would hurt working people. The letter gives no information about their pay, and it never suggests new hours.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: More and more schools offer night classes.

quiz.q: How many schools offer night classes today?
Tap the sentence that explains WHY the students choose evening lessons.
